tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README explains the purpose of this repository: it is the React web frontend for the Greenstand Treetracker Admin Panel, the tool staff use to verify, process, and manage data collected by the Treetracker mobile app. It also flags a key architectural fact that shapes the whole codebase: the app is mid-migration from one legacy dedicated API to several focused Greenstand microservices (treetracker-api, earnings-api, field-data, query-api, regions-api, reporting, stakeholder-api). The package.json manifest backs this up concretely, listing Material UI and Redux/Rematch as the UI and state-management foundations and create-react-app as the build tooling.

tour.title: Application Bootstrap
tour.description: src/index.js is the true entry point: it renders the React tree into the DOM and registers the service worker. It immediately delegates setup work to src/init.js, which configures cross-cutting concerns (like error/logging setup) before src/App.js takes over as the root component. Reading these three files in sequence shows you the startup order every request to the app follows, before any feature code runs.

tour.title: Routing and Global Providers
tour.description: Routers.js declares every top-level route (Verify, Growers, Messaging, Species, Payments, Earnings, Stakeholders and more), wiring each URL to its page component and gating private routes behind authentication. It sits inside AppContext, the single most depended-upon module in the codebase (26 incoming references), which holds global app state such as the logged-in user, organization, and shared UI flags. theme.js supplies the Material UI theme consumed everywhere, so this step is where the app's global scaffolding -- routing, shared state, and visual styling -- comes together.

tour.title: API / Service Layer
tour.description: treeTrackerApi.js is the central API client, exposing methods for fetching and mutating captures, growers, species, and tags against the underlying services. apiUtils.js provides the shared request helpers (auth headers, base URL resolution, error handling) that every API module builds on. growers.js shows the pattern in practice: a focused module per microservice domain, here wrapping grower CRUD, registrations, and selfie lookups behind small typed functions that UI code can call without knowing about HTTP details.

tour.title: The Context / State Pattern
tour.description: Beyond the global AppContext from Step 3, each feature area gets its own React Context provider that owns data fetching and local state for that slice of the app. CapturesContext manages the capture list, pagination, ordering, and filter counts; VerifyContext layers the verification workflow on top (paginated image loading, selection tracking, approve/reject actions); CaptureDetailContext fetches the deeper detail (species, tags, tokenization) for a single selected capture. This is the recurring architectural pattern you will see repeated for every feature vertical in the app: a Context provider wraps API calls from Step 4 and exposes clean state and actions to components.

tour.title: Feature Vertical: Capture Verification
tour.description: Verify.js is the main verification page, rendering the responsive grid of capture images and wiring up selection, pinning, and detail actions. CaptureFilter.js is the sidebar filter form (grower, device, dates, species, tags, verification status) that narrows the capture list. CaptureTable.js renders captures in tabular form for bulk review. Together these three components show how a UI feature consumes the Context layer from Step 5 to build a full workflow screen -- this is the pattern to recognize when reading any other feature area (Growers, Species, Payments) in the codebase.

tour.title: The Filter Domain Model
tour.description: Filter.js is a plain model class, not a React component, that encapsulates capture search criteria and knows how to turn itself into an API 'where' query object -- this is what CaptureFilter.js from Step 6 actually builds and passes to CapturesContext. FilterGrower.js is the sibling model for grower search criteria, following the same getWhereObj convention, and the codebase has equivalent FilterRegion and FilterStakeholder classes for their respective domains. auth.js rounds out the data layer with permission-checking helpers (hasPermission, session) used throughout the UI to gate actions by role. Recognizing this Filter-per-domain convention is key to navigating the rest of the app's data layer.

tour.title: Feature Vertical: Messaging
tour.description: MessagingContext follows the same provider pattern from Step 5, but for the messaging domain: it loads threads, authors, and regions on mount and exposes them to the UI. messaging.js is its API client, exposing region lookup, author listing, message CRUD, and bulk/announcement sends. Messaging.js is the top-level page that coordinates the inbox and thread view, while MessageBody.js renders the actual conversation, handling plain messages, announcements, and survey responses as distinct bubble types. This second full feature vertical reinforces the Context-plus-API-plus-page pattern while showing a materially different UI shape (chat-style) from the tabular Captures workflow in Step 6.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipeline
tour.description: treetracker-frontend-pr.yml runs on every pull request: it installs dependencies, lints, and builds the client to catch problems before merge. build_and_release.yaml runs on every push to resolve a deploy channel and AWS secrets, build the client, cut a semantic-release version, and deploy the bundle to a dev CDN. deploy.yaml is the manually-triggered counterpart used to promote a specific build to staging or production by syncing the bundle to the target environment's S3/CloudFront setup. Together these three workflows show the full path from a code change to a running deployment.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use `on` to declare triggers (push, pull_request, or manual workflow_dispatch), `jobs` for parallel units of work, and `steps` for sequential commands within a job. Splitting PR validation (fast, every push) from release/deploy (slower, gated) keeps feedback quick while still automating the full release path.

tour.title: Testing Strategy: Jest and Cypress
tour.description: verify.test.js is a large Jest/React Testing Library suite exercising the Verify page end-to-end within the test runner: capture selection, approval/rejection, and filter interactions, all against mocked API responses. capturesFilter.spec.py.js is a genuine Cypress end-to-end test that drives the Captures page filter UI in a real browser, covering the same filtering behavior from Step 6 but through actual user interaction. Filter.spec.py.js is a Cypress component test, a middle tier that mounts a single component (here the Filter drawer) with a mocked Redux store and Material UI theme, verifying it in isolation without a full page or backend. Together these three layers -- unit/integration via Jest, isolated component tests, and full browser E2E via Cypress -- form the project's testing pyramid.
